# tulpa <img src="man/figures/logo.svg" align="right" height="139" alt="tulpa logo" />

*Bayesian hierarchical models for grouped, spatial and temporal data*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/tulpa)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=tulpa)
[![CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/tulpa)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tulpa)
[![Monthly downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/tulpa)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tulpa)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpa/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpa/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/tulpa/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/tulpa)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

tulpa fits Bayesian hierarchical models in R, including models for counts, proportions, repeated measurements, and observations distributed across space or time.

A formula describes how measured predictors and unobserved effects contribute to the response. The engine combines these effects with an observation distribution and fits the model using nested Laplace approximation or Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Its numerical routines are written in templated C++. The result includes posterior estimates, uncertainty intervals, and diagnostics that help you assess the fit.

tulpa supports:

- **Grouped effects.** Random intercepts and slopes, including uncertainty in their variances and correlations.
- **Smooth, spatial and temporal structure.** Smooth covariate effects, spatial fields, temporal processes, and combinations of these structures.
- **Several inference methods.** Deterministic approximations, MCMC sampling, and correction methods are selected through the same fitting function.
- **Custom models.** Model-specific observation likelihoods and custom latent processes are supplied through R or C++ interfaces.

[Calibration](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/sbc.html) shows how to assess posterior calibration through repeated simulations. [Reliability diagnostics](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/reliability-pareto-k.html) explains what can be checked on an individual fit. The package is experimental and its interface may change.

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

```r
install.packages("tulpa")
```

CRAN provides binaries for Windows and macOS, which need no build tools.

The development version compiles C++17 code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) matching your R version |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```r
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Then install tulpa from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/tulpa")
```

The build links against the BLAS and LAPACK libraries that R itself uses for matrix operations, so no other system library is needed. Package dependencies, including [tulpaMesh](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=tulpaMesh) for spatial mesh construction, are installed with tulpa.

### Optional: multithreading

OpenMP lets the nested-Laplace fitters use several CPU threads through `n_threads` in their `control` list. The [single-process](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/reference/tulpa_nested_laplace.html) and [joint-model](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/reference/tulpa_nested_laplace_joint.html) reference pages describe the available controls.

Rtools on Windows and the default compiler on Linux include OpenMP. Without it, the package installs and runs on one thread.

#### macOS setup

Apple's compiler needs an additional OpenMP runtime. Install it in Terminal:

```sh
brew install libomp
```

Before installing tulpa from source, add the settings for your Mac to `~/.R/Makevars`, R's personal compiler-settings file. Create the directory and file if needed.

**Apple Silicon:**

```makefile
CPPFLAGS += -I/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/lib -lomp
```

**Intel:**

```makefile
CPPFLAGS += -I/usr/local/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/usr/local/opt/libomp/lib -lomp
```

## Usage

1. Fit a model with `tulpa()`.
2. Inspect the estimates and inference method with `summary()`.
3. Extract the group effects with `ranef()`.

The built-in `InsectSprays` data contain insect counts and the spray treatment used for each observation. This Poisson model gives each treatment a random intercept, estimating its effect relative to the overall log count.

```{r usage, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)

fit <- tulpa(
  count ~ (1 | spray),
  data = InsectSprays,
  family = "poisson"
)
summary(fit)
```

```{r group-effects, results = "hide"}
effects <- ranef(fit)
```

```{r group-effects-table, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
knitr::kable(
  effects[c("term", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")],
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Treatment", "Estimate", "Lower", "Upper")
)
```

Supply a data frame with the response, predictors, and grouping variables named in the formula. Choose an observation family appropriate to the response. [Data formatting](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/data-formatting.html) covers response encodings, grouping variables, and spatial inputs.

## Random effects, smoothers, and fields

Formula terms describe the model structure. `(1 | group)` adds random intercepts, `(1 + x | group)` adds correlated random intercepts and slopes, and `s(x)` adds a smooth covariate effect. Spatial and temporal specifications describe dependence between locations or times.

[Random slopes and covariances](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/random-slopes.html) walks through inference for group-level variances and correlations. The [spatial](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/spatial-models.html) and [temporal](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/temporal-models.html) articles show how to supply the corresponding structures.

## Inference and diagnostics

Automatic mode selects an inference method and records its reason on the fit. An explicit mode selects MCMC, Laplace approximation, or variational inference; variational methods require an explicit choice. [Inference modes](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/inference-modes.html) describes the methods and the models each supports.

Diagnostics depend on how the posterior was computed. MCMC fits report chain convergence and effective sample sizes. Approximation fits report the available integration and inner-approximation checks. [Reliability diagnostics](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/reliability-pareto-k.html) explains how to interpret these results and their limits.

## Custom models and processes

Companion packages supply observation likelihoods and reuse tulpa's inference and latent structures. [tulpaObs](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpaObs) provides models for occupancy, abundance, and detection; [tulpaRatio](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpaRatio) provides models for ratios, rates, and proportions.

For a custom Gaussian latent process, supply its precision matrix and mean through R functions or a compiled C++ definition. The [custom-process tutorial](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/tgmrf.html) shows both interfaces. The [EM + Laplace article](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/em-laplace.html) describes the shared fitting framework for models with unobserved observation states.

## Documentation

Start with the [quickstart](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/quickstart.html): a complete path from a formula to a fitted model.

- [Data formatting](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/data-formatting.html): response encodings, grouping variables and spatial inputs.
- [Random slopes and covariances](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/random-slopes.html): group-level variances and correlations.
- [Spatial models](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/spatial-models.html) and [temporal models](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/temporal-models.html): supplying dependence between locations or times.
- [Inference modes](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/inference-modes.html): the inference methods and the models each supports.
- [Priors](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/priors.html): prior distributions for coefficients and latent structures.
- [Reliability diagnostics](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/reliability-pareto-k.html): what can be checked on an individual fit.
- [Calibration](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/sbc.html): posterior calibration through repeated simulations.
- [Model comparison](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/model-comparison.html): comparing fitted models and combining predictions.
- [Checkpoint and resume](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/checkpoint.html): saving and continuing sampling runs.
- [Custom latent processes](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/tgmrf.html) and [EM + Laplace](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/articles/em-laplace.html): extending the engine.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/reference/): every function, grouped by job.

## Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpa/issues). A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/), and the output of `sessionInfo()`.

## Citation

```{r citation, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cit <- citation("tulpa")
fence <- function(lang, x) cat("```", lang, "\n", paste(x, collapse = "\n\n"), "\n```\n\n", sep = "")
cat(attr(cit, "mheader"), "\n\n", sep = "")
fence("text", format(cit, style = "text"))
cat("BibTeX:\n\n")
fence("bibtex", format(cit, style = "bibtex"))
```

Download the citation as [BibTeX](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/tulpa.bib) or [RIS](https://gillescolling.com/tulpa/tulpa.ris).
